clinical_knowledge.topic: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: facial rash, joint pain, hair loss, and fatigue worsening over 3 months
Key HPI features: 29F presents with 3 months of worsening fatigue, pain in hand and wrist joints, increased hair shedding, and a red rash across her cheeks and nose that flares up after sun exposure.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Dermatomyositis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Foamy urine or swelling — kidney involvement.
management_principles: Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
: Check ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith antibodies, complement levels, and urinalysis (to screen for lupus nephritis)

Prompt rheumatology-directed management is required; emergency assessment is needed for nephritis, neurologic symptoms, chest pain/dyspnea, severe cytopenia symptoms, or other organ-threatening disease.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). facial rash, joint pain, hair loss, and fatigue worsening over 3 months. 29F presents with 3 months of worsening fatigue, pain in hand and wrist joints, increased hair shedding, and a red rash across her cheeks and nose that flares up after sun exposure.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
reference_soap.plan: Confirm the syndrome with targeted testing rather than ANA alone: CBC, creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis with microscopy and urine protein quantification, complements, anti-dsDNA, and other serology as clinically indicated. Urgent same-day assessment is needed for reduced urine output, edema/foamy urine, hypertension, neurologic symptoms, chest pain/dyspnea, or severe illness. Rheumatology should direct hydroxychloroquine, glucocorticoids, or immunosuppressants with pregnancy planning, eye screening, infection review, and laboratory monitoring.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for facial rash, joint pain, hair loss, and fatigue worsening over 3 months
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for rheumatology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).

teaching.one_liner: A multisystem autoimmune disease causing a sun-sensitive facial rash, joint pain, hair loss, and fatigue — needs screening for internal organ, especially kidney, involvement.
red_flags: Foamy urine or swelling — kidney involvement

must_ask.say: Does your facial rash worsen with sun exposure?
How much hair are you losing?
How many months has this been going on?

history.answer: My hands and wrists have been aching and I've developed this red rash across my cheeks and nose over the past three months.
The pain is mainly in both of my wrists and the knuckles of both hands, pretty much symmetrically on both sides.
It started gradually about three months ago and has steadily gotten worse over time.
It's a persistent dull, throbbing ache that feels like a 4 or 5 out of 10 on most days.
Yes, my knuckles and wrists look slightly puffy and feel warm to the touch, especially when I wake up.
My hands feel very stiff every morning when I wake up, and it takes about an hour or two of moving around before they loosen up.
Moving my hands gently helps relieve the morning stiffness, but typing or doing heavy hand work for a long time makes the aching worse.
I have trouble opening tight jars and typing my graduate thesis because my fingers feel sore and weak, but I can walk normally without problems.
The red rash spread across both my cheeks and over the bridge of my nose, and it gets noticeably redder and burns after I spend time out in the sun.
Yes, over the past couple of months, huge clumps of hair come out in my brush and shower drain.
Now that you mention it, I noticed a tiny sore on the roof of my mouth last week, though it doesn't really hurt. My eyes have also felt a bit gritty lately.
I don't have high fevers or shaking chills, but I frequently feel warm like I have a low-grade fever, and I am completely exhausted every single day.
No, my urine looks normal with no foam or blood, and I haven't noticed any swelling in my legs or puffy eyes.
No, I haven't injured my hands or wrists, and I don't feel any clicking, locking, or giving way.
No, this is the very first time I've ever experienced joint pain like this.
No, I don't have back pain, heel pain, or swollen sausage-like toes.
No, I haven't had diarrhea, painful urination, vaginal discharge, or a sore throat recently.
I eat a balanced diet and haven't had unusual binge meals with meat or seafood, and I don't take any water pills.
No, I've never taken steroids or immunosuppressant drugs, and I've never had injections or surgery in my joints.
I am in a monogamous relationship with my partner and haven't had any new sexual partners or unusual symptoms.
I've read online that a rash like this with joint pain and hair loss could be a severe allergy or maybe lupus.
I'm really worried that this might be an autoimmune disease damaging my kidneys or other internal organs, and I hope we can run thorough tests today.
I don't have any chronic illnesses or high blood pressure, and I've always been healthy before this.
I've never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I'm not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter pain relievers, or herbal supplements.
I don't have any known allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic vapes.
I might drink one glass of wine every few weeks socially, but nothing regularly.
I'm a graduate student working on my master's degree, and I live in an apartment with my partner.
Nobody in my immediate family has lupus or rheumatoid arthritis, although my mother has a sluggish thyroid.
My last period was about two weeks ago; my cycles are regular every 28 days, I use condoms, and there's no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 37.1°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
The patient appears mildly tired but is comfortable and in no acute distress.
Erythematous maculopapular rash across both malar eminences and the nasal bridge with sparing of the nasolabial folds, along with diffuse non-scarring scalp hair thinning.
A small, shallow, painless ulcer on the hard palate, with no mucosal bleeding or tonsillar enlargement.
Mild soft-tissue swelling, warmth, and tenderness to palpation across bilateral metacarpophalangeal, proximal interphalangeal, and wrist joints without joint deformity.
Normal heart sounds with regular rhythm and no murmurs, gallops, or pericardial friction rub.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with no crackles, wheezes, or pleural friction rubs.
Soft, non-tender abdomen without organomegaly, masses, or fluid wave.
No pretibial or pedal edema on either leg, and peripheral pulses are full and symmetric.
